content: Equine influenza, commonly referred to as horse flu, is caused by specific strains of Influenza A virus that are endemic in horses. The virus was first isolated in 1956. There are two primary subtypes of the virus: equine-1 (H7N7), which often affects the heart muscle of horses, and equine-2 (H3N8), which is generally associated with more severe disease. This disease is widespread globally and has an almost 100% infection rate in unvaccinated horse populations that have not been previously exposed to the virus. The incubation period for equine influenza ranges from one to five days. Horses infected with this virus may exhibit symptoms such as fever, a dry hacking cough, nasal discharge, depression, and a reluctance to eat or drink. However, most affected horses recover within two to three weeks. Vaccination protocols typically involve an initial course of two doses administered three to six weeks apart, followed by booster doses at intervals of six to twelve months. However, it is widely acknowledged that in many cases, these schedules may not sustain protective antibody levels, and more frequent vaccinations are recommended in high-risk situations. In Britain, it is common practice for horses participating in shows to be vaccinated against equine influenza, and proof of vaccination is often required. The Fédération Equestre Internationale (FEI) mandates vaccination every six months. In August 2007, a significant outbreak of equine influenza occurred in Australia, a country that had previously been free of the virus.
